title: Two fathers: the world Ishvara makes, the world the mind makes
hook: Two fathers, one false report: the Panchadashi puts grief in the world the mind builds, not the world Ishvara makes.
carry: ishvara makes the world; the mind makes the grief
tomorrow: a painted scene on a starched cloth. where did the cloth go?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Indra went back again and again, and the Panchadashi named the witness self that stays through waking, dream and sleep. Today, two fathers, and a message that changes everything without changing anything.

A screenshot goes around saying someone got fired. It isn't true. They spend the night sick about it anyway. The Panchadashi tells an older version. A son has gone abroad. A traveler brings his father news: your son has died. The father weeps. But the report was false; the son is alive and well. Meanwhile another father's son really has died far away, and someone tells him the boy is doing fine. That father goes about his day untroubled. So what, exactly, made the first man grieve?
screen: `A FALSE SCREENSHOT, A REAL NIGHT.` → `TWO FATHERS, TWO REPORTS.` → `WHAT MADE HIM GRIEVE?`

segments.voice: The chapter draws a line between two kinds of making. Vedanta calls them Ishvara's creation and the jiva's creation. There's the world as Ishvara, the Lord, makes it: the son himself, the road, the far country. And there's the world each person, each jiva, builds on top of it in the mind: my son, gone; my son, safe. The grief came from the picture the father was holding, not from the son. A second example: one gem on a table. One person who gets it is delighted, one who loses it is crushed, a third hardly notices. The gem doesn't change. The minds around it do. So bondage, the book says, lives in that second world. It doesn't ask anyone to pretend the outer world isn't there; a real son still matters. Meet the world as the Lord made it, and hold your own pictures lightly. Seeing that layer clearly is a step toward knowing the witness self. Now the week, in one breath. A father who says look again. The Vedas, breathed out and heard. A debate over rites and knowing. The Lord, met in the heart. One clay in every pot. Indra, past body, dream and sleep. And a father's tears over a picture.
screen: `ISHVARA'S WORLD: AS IT'S GIVEN.` · `THE JIVA'S WORLD: WHAT THE MIND LAYS OVER IT.` · `ONE GEM, THREE REACTIONS.` · then, large: `THE GRIEF WAS IN THE PICTURE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let one small worry about something that hasn't happened come to mind. Notice the picture the mind has built around it, the faces, the words, the ending. Then let the picture be just a picture, and come back to the breath, which is happening right now.
The Panchadashi: a book of Advaita verses. Here, it splits the world as it's given from the world the mind lays on top.
Keep this one: Ishvara makes the world; the mind makes the grief. That's a week of knowing.

fork.setup: one gem sits on a table. one person gets it and is delighted; one loses it and is crushed; one hardly notices. what changed?
options: only the minds around it; the gem is the same.
the gem's value went up and down with each owner.
nothing at all; all three feel the same inside.
fork.reveal: The Panchadashi's point: the gem doesn't change. The world each mind builds around it does, and that's where the joy and the grief live.

original.note: Sanskrit Ishvara, the Lord; in this chapter, the maker of the world as it's given, apart from the mind's own layer.

chat.meaning: The first father wept over a false report; his grief came from the picture he held, not his son. The Panchadashi separates the world Ishvara makes from the world the jiva's mind builds, and places bondage in the second.

jiva.meaning: the individual self, which builds its own inner world
